name: property-based-serializer
intent: Keep the type or format hint that selects a deserialiser in the message's metadata - properties, headers or other envelope fields - rather than inside the payload, so that receivers and intermediaries can classify, route and dispatch a message without parsing its body.
problem: One channel or topic carries several message types and the receiver must decide which deserialiser or handler applies. If that decision needs the body, every router, filter and consumer pays the full parse cost, and brokers - which index metadata, not payload - cannot route on it at all. The recurring trigger: one channel, many types, and a cheap classification decision needed before the body is read.
context: Applies wherever the transport supplies a metadata section that travels with the message and is readable before the body: JMS properties and message selectors, AMQP basic properties and headers (headers exchanges), Kafka record headers, MQTT 5 user properties, gRPC metadata, HTTP headers, or a fixed protocol header such as netlink's nlmsg_type. It is the right choice when routing, filtering, version negotiation or polymorphic deserialisation must be decided cheaply and uniformly and the metadata channel is preserved end to end.
benefits: Classification and routing become a lookup on a small, indexed field: a broker-side selector, subscription rule or consumer-side registry can pick the deserialiser or handler without buffering or parsing the body.
One channel can carry heterogeneous payloads: types are distinguished by the hint, so a single topic or queue no longer needs one destination per type or a schema-registry round trip to disambiguate.
The hint is a contract independent of the payload encoding: it survives a change of body format (JSON today, Avro tomorrow) as long as the token vocabulary is preserved.
Intermediaries stay cheap: content-based routers, filters and claim-check style components need only the metadata section, which client libraries usually already materialise.

Polymorphic deserialisation becomes explicit and auditable: the token-to-type mapping is one allowlist, so the set of accepted types is a reviewable configuration rather than an implicit consequence of a payload field.

A governed hint improves the security posture: a closed registry rejects unknown tokens before any parser runs, avoiding the trial-deserialisation and gadget-class failure modes of content-driven typing.
tradeoffs: Hint and body can disagree, and nothing on the wire forces them to match; unless the token is written by the same step that writes the body, the receiver silently deserialises into the wrong type.

Header semantics are transport-specific and not portable: a JMS property is a typed primitive with reserved JMSX/JMS_ prefixes, an AMQP header is a typed map, a Kafka header is a repeated byte array, an MQTT 5 user property is a UTF-8 pair, and a bridge maps only a fixed subset - so moving a message between transports can drop or mangle the hint (MQTT 3.1.1 has no user properties at all).
Tooling can strip the metadata: some deserialisers remove type headers after use by default, and republishing pipelines often copy only key and value, so a forwarded message arrives unclassified.
The token is a second externally visible contract that must be versioned, documented and governed alongside the schema, which is real ongoing coordination cost.

Header-driven type selection is a classic attack surface when the token may name arbitrary classes or assemblies (unsafe polymorphic typing, deserialisation gadgets); the registry must be a closed allowlist and the trust boundary must be explicit.
A missing token needs an explicit policy, and the tempting fallbacks - a default type or trial deserialisation - are both silent-corruption paths.
The payload stops being self-describing: replaying raw bytes from a store or file dump without their metadata loses the ability to select a reader.

participants.responsibility: Writes the hint and the body in one step so the token always describes the payload actually sent; owns the token vocabulary together with the consumers.
Carries the metadata section (properties/headers) alongside an opaque body; the transport guarantees both travel together or fails.
Maps a token to a concrete deserialiser or type; a closed allowlist that rejects unknown tokens before any parser runs.
Reads the hint first, resolves it in the registry and parses the body exactly once, with the parser the hint selected.
Consumes only the metadata section - broker rule, message selector, consumer-side filter - to route, drop or prioritise messages without touching the body.
The agreed, versioned set of token values and their meanings, shared by producers, routers and consumers so the same token means the same type everywhere.

use_cases: A Kafka topic carrying several event types: consumers register a per-token deserialiser and stream processors route on the record header.
JMS or AMQP queues with message selectors, where the provider evaluates the property and delivers only messages whose type the consumer can handle.
An AMQP headers exchange where the type header is itself the routing criterion, leaving the routing key free for other dimensions.
Multi-version rollouts: old and new consumers share one channel and pick a reader by a format or version token instead of guessing from the body.
Protocol-level dispatch where the receiving stack picks a handler from the header before decoding - netlink's nlmsg_type, or gRPC metadata consumed by an interceptor or proxy.
Polyglot pipelines where a registry id or format token in the header selects a per-format parser while the payload stays opaque to the transport.

Spring for Apache Kafka's JsonSerializer and JsonDeserializer put type information in Kafka record headers, and its delegating serializer/deserializer selects a codec from a header token while the JSON value remains unchanged.
RabbitMQ's headers exchange routes messages by header key/value matches (x-match any/all), allowing a format or type property to route an opaque payload without using the routing key.
avoid_when: The metadata section is not preserved end to end (MQTT 3.1.1 has no user properties; some bridges and tooling strip headers) - carry the hint in the payload instead (content-based serializer) or in an envelope that is part of the body.
Messages are archived or replayed as raw bytes without their metadata: a self-describing payload is the safer choice.
The type is already implied by the destination (one queue or topic per type) - a datatype channel is simpler and needs no vocabulary.
The classification depends on payload values (a field's value decides the handler) - that is content-based routing, not a metadata hint.
A single message type reaches a single consumer with no routing: a direct typed deserialiser call is enough.
anti_patterns: Setting the type token in a different place from the serialisation step (or defaulting it), so hint and payload drift apart and the receiver deserialises into the wrong type without an error.
Token values that name implementation classes or assemblies directly and are accepted from untrusted senders - the classic unsafe-polymorphism and deserialisation-gadget hole.
Trial deserialisation as the primary strategy: trying every parser until one succeeds makes failures silent and reduces the hint to decoration.
A per-team token vocabulary with no shared registry, so the same token means different types on either side of a channel.
Trusting a header that a bridge, forwarder or deserialiser rewrites or drops, so messages arrive unclassified and the fallback path decides their type.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: classification metadata versus payload data - the envelope decides who reads the body, the body never decides who reads it.
Explicit published contract: the token vocabulary is a documented, versioned interface rather than an implementation detail of a payload class.
Open/closed principle: a new message type arrives by registering a token, not by editing every consumer or router.
Fail fast at the boundary: an unknown or missing token is rejected before any parser runs.
Least privilege / closed by default: only registered tokens map to types; the sender never gets to choose an arbitrary class.
best_practices: Emit the token from the same code path that serialises the body, so the hint cannot disagree with the payload.
Use stable, technology-neutral token values (a short name or registry id such as `order-created`), never implementation class or assembly names.
Keep the registry a closed allowlist and fail fast on unknown or missing tokens; make the missing-token policy explicit instead of silently defaulting.
Version the vocabulary and treat token removal or re-meaning as a breaking change; document which token maps to which schema version.
Keep the hint small and cheap to read - it is on the routing hot path - and do not duplicate payload data into the headers.
Test the wire contract, not just the classes: assert that the emitted token survives the broker or bridge and that unknown tokens are rejected.
If messages are archived or replayed, store the token with them or fall back to a self-describing reader.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (2003) - Format Indicator, in the Message Construction chapter; its three alternatives are Version Number, Foreign Key and Format Document.
